title: Potential energy curves
examples: How do I tell if an object is in stable equilibrium from a graph?
What does the minimum point on an energy curve mean for an object?
Can you explain the difference between stable and unstable equilibrium using a real object?

explain.say: Today we are looking at potential energy curves. These curves help us understand where an object likes to sit.
The point where the curve is flat means the object is at equilibrium. This is where the net force is zero.
If the curve is at a minimum, the equilibrium is stable. The object wants to return to that spot.
If the curve is at a maximum, the equilibrium is unstable. The object will move away from this point.
Consider a ball placed at the bottom of a bowl. This is a real-life example of stable equilibrium.

draw.text: Real Life: Ball in a Bowl

explain.say: A common mistake is thinking all flat spots are stable. Remember, a flat spot at a peak is unstable.

faq.q: What does the shape of the curve tell me about the force?
faq.a: The slope of the potential energy curve tells you the force acting on the object. A steep slope means a large force.
asks: How is force related to the graph?
Does the steepness show the force?

faq.q: If the curve is flat, does that mean there is no force?
faq.a: Yes, a flat section means the potential energy is not changing, so the net force acting on the object is zero.
asks: When is the net force zero?

faq.q: How can I tell if an equilibrium is stable just by looking at the graph?
faq.a: If the curve is at a minimum value, the equilibrium is stable. The object will tend to return to that minimum.

faq.q: Is a point of zero potential energy always stable?
faq.a: No, a point of zero potential energy could be a maximum or a minimum. You must check the second derivative or the surrounding curve shape.
asks: Can PE be zero at an unstable point?

faq.q: What happens if I push an object slightly away from an unstable equilibrium?
faq.a: If you push it slightly, the object will accelerate away from the equilibrium point because the force pushes it further away.
asks: Will it fall away from the top?

facts: Equilibrium is a point where the net force acting on an object is zero.
A minimum in the potential energy curve corresponds to stable equilibrium.
A maximum in the potential energy curve corresponds to unstable equilibrium.
The slope of the potential energy curve represents the restoring force.

quiz.say: If the potential energy curve has a minimum at x equals two, what type of equilibrium is present?
quiz.why: A minimum in the potential energy curve indicates that the object has a tendency to return to that point, which is stable equilibrium.

wrong.0: Neutral equilibrium happens when the energy curve is flat everywhere, not just at one point.
wrong.1: This is too general; 'Stable' is the specific classification required by the curve's shape.
wrong.3: This is wrong because unstable equilibrium occurs at the highest points of the curve.

quiz.say: At what point on a potential energy graph is the net force on an object zero?

options.show: Where the curve crosses the x-axis
options.say: Where the curve crosses the x-axis

quiz.why: Force is the negative gradient of potential energy; therefore, where the curve is horizontal, the force is zero, meaning equilibrium.

wrong.0: While the lowest point is often an equilibrium, the force can be zero at other points too.
wrong.1: The highest point is an equilibrium, but the force is not zero there unless it is a maximum.
wrong.2: Crossing the x-axis only means the potential energy is zero, not that the force is zero.

quiz.say: A ball balanced perfectly on top of a hill represents which type of equilibrium?
quiz.why: The top of the hill is a maximum point on the potential energy curve, meaning any small displacement results in a force pushing it away.

wrong.0: Neutral equilibrium means the object stays wherever it is placed, which is not the case on a hill.
wrong.1: This is not a type of equilibrium; it describes the force, not the state.
wrong.3: Stable equilibrium occurs at the bottom of a dip, not the top of a hill.
